stem: How is a pre-determined overhead absorption rate calculated?

options.rationale: Correct: both figures are forecasts made before the period.
That uses figures known only after the period ends.
A rate mixes forecast and actual figures here.
It mixes actual cost with a forecast of activity.

explanation: The rate is fixed in advance from the budgeted overhead and the budgeted activity so that jobs can be costed and priced during the period.

stem: Which absorption base is most suitable for a highly mechanised bottling department with few workers?

options.rationale: Correct: the overhead is caused by the use of machines.
Few workers means labour hours say little about the overhead.
Labour cost is low and not linked to the machine overheads.
Material cost would distort the share of overhead.

explanation: The base should reflect what causes the overhead. In a machine-intensive department that is machine hours.

stem: Why do businesses use budgeted rather than actual overhead to cost jobs?

options.content: Budgeted overhead is always exactly equal to actual overhead
options.rationale: The two usually differ, which gives over- or under-absorption.

options.content: Actual overhead is known only after the period ends
options.rationale: Correct: prices are needed now, and a pre-determined rate allows quotations and steady costs.

options.content: Actual overhead is never recorded in the ledger accounts
options.rationale: Actual overhead is recorded; it is simply known later.

options.content: The law requires a budgeted rate to be used in all cases
options.rationale: No law requires it.

explanation: Jobs must be priced before the year ends. A pre-determined rate also avoids seasonal changes in the cost of a job.

stem: A department budgets overheads of US\$36,000, 9,000 direct labour hours and 12,000 machine hours. Overheads are absorbed on direct labour hours. What is the absorption rate?

options.rationale: This divides by the machine hours, not the labour hours.
This adds two different bases together.
This halves the correct rate for no reason.

explanation: The base is direct labour hours, so the rate is 36,000 ÷ 9,000 = US\$4 per direct labour hour.
hints: Use the budgeted activity that matches the base.

stem: A workshop budgets overheads of US\$33,600 and direct labour cost of US\$48,000. A job has direct labour cost of US\$900. How much overhead is absorbed by the job if overheads are absorbed as a percentage of direct labour cost?

options.rationale: This divides the labour cost by the rate instead of multiplying.
Correct: 70% of 900.
This divides the overhead by the labour cost of the job.
This adds the overhead to the labour cost; the question asks for the overhead alone.

hints: Rate = budgeted overhead ÷ budgeted direct labour cost.

stem: A factory makes one standard product, a 2-litre bottle of cooking oil. Which absorption base is simplest and suitable?

options.rationale: Needs cost data that is not necessary for identical units.

options.content: A rate per machine hour for each department
options.rationale: Possible, but more complex than needed for one product.
Correct: every unit receives the same share.

options.content: A rate per square metre of floor area
options.rationale: Floor area is an apportionment basis, not an absorption base.

explanation: With one standard product a rate per unit is simplest and accurate.

stem: A factory changes its absorption base from direct labour hours to machine hours. Job X uses many machine hours and few labour hours. What happens to the overhead and cost of Job X?

options.content: Less overhead is absorbed, so the cost of X falls
options.rationale: A machine-intensive job carries more overhead under machine hours.

options.content: The overhead is unchanged because the factory total is fixed
options.rationale: The total is fixed but its distribution among jobs changes.

options.content: More overhead is absorbed, so the cost of X rises
options.rationale: Correct: the job takes a larger share of the overhead under the new base.

options.content: Overhead is absorbed twice, so the cost of X doubles
options.rationale: Only one base is used.

explanation: The total overhead is unchanged but the share carried by each job depends on the base. A machine-intensive job carries more when machine hours are used.
hints: Which job uses the factory's machines most?

stem: A departmental absorption rate is generally more accurate than a single rate for the whole factory when departments use labour and machines differently.
explanation: True. Departmental rates reflect the different cost of overhead and activity of each department.

stem: A business can choose an absorption base that makes the total overhead of the factory larger or smaller.
explanation: False. The base changes how a given total is shared among jobs, not the total itself.
hints: Is the total changed or only its distribution?

stem: Match each absorption base to the department for which it is most suitable.

right.content: A department of automatic bottling machines
A hand-finishing department with workers on different shifts
A business making one identical product
A tailoring department where wage rates are the same for all workers

explanation: The base should follow the cause of overhead: machines, hours of labour, units of an identical product, or labour cost where wage rates are similar.

stem: A Gweru plastics factory budgets production overheads of US\$63,000 for the year, 10,500 machine hours and 14,000 direct labour hours. Overheads are absorbed on machine hours. Calculate the absorption rate per machine hour.
explanation: 63,000 ÷ 10,500 = US\$6 per machine hour. Dividing by the direct labour hours gives US\$4.50, which is the rate for a different base.
workedSolution: 1. 63,000 ÷ 10,500 = US\$6 per machine hour. Dividing by the direct labour hours gives US\$4.50, which is the rate for a different base.
hints: Divide by the hours that match the base.

stem: A Masvingo clothing factory budgets overheads of US\$54,000 and direct labour cost of US\$72,000. Calculate the overhead absorption rate as a percentage of direct labour cost, to one decimal place.
explanation: 54,000 ÷ 72,000 × 100 = 75.0%. Inverting the fraction gives the labour cost as a percentage of overhead.
workedSolution: 1. 54,000 ÷ 72,000 × 100 = 75.0%. Inverting the fraction gives the labour cost as a percentage of overhead.

stem: Using the rate per machine hour from the first numerical question, calculate the production overhead absorbed by a batch of mugs that uses 15.5 machine hours.
explanation: Overhead absorbed = 15.5 × 6.00 = US\$93. Using the labour hour rate (US\$4.50) would be wrong because the base is machine hours.
workedSolution: 1. Overhead absorbed = 15.5 × 6.00 = US\$93. Using the labour hour rate (US\$4.50) would be wrong because the base is machine hours.
hints: Multiply the rate by the machine hours used.

stem: A job uses direct materials of US\$410, 18 direct labour hours paid at US\$5 an hour and 6 machine hours. Overheads are absorbed at US\$6 per machine hour. Calculate the total production cost of the job.
explanation: Prime cost = 410 + 18 × 5 = 500. Overhead = 6 × 6 = 36. Total production cost = US\$536.
workedSolution: 1. Prime cost = 410 + 18 × 5 = 500. Overhead = 6 × 6 = 36. Total production cost = US\$536.
hints: Prime cost first, then add the absorbed overhead.

stem: Explain why a business uses a pre-determined absorption rate rather than waiting for actual overheads.

points.description: Prices and quotations are needed before the actual overhead for the period is known
A budgeted rate avoids large changes in the cost of a job caused by the month in which it is made

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Quotations are needed during the period, before the actual overheads are known. A fixed rate also stops the cost of the same job rising in a month when overheads are high.

explanation: One mark for each reason.

stem: Explain why a departmental absorption rate may give a more accurate cost than one rate for the whole factory.

points.description: Departments have different overheads and use different amounts of labour and machines
Jobs spend different time in each department
A rate for each department charges the job according to the resources it actually uses

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Departments differ in the machines and labour they use. A job that spends time only in the cheap department should carry less overhead, which departmental rates do.

explanation: One mark for each point.
hints: Think of a job that passes through only one department.

stem: Evaluate the use of direct labour hours as the absorption base in a workshop that has recently bought automatic cutting machines.

points.description: The machines now cause much of the overhead (depreciation, power)
Labour hours are less related to the cause of overhead, so jobs that use many machine hours are under-costed
Machine hours (or separate rates for machines and hand work) would be fairer
Under-costing can lead to prices that are too low and unprofitable work accepted

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Machines now cause the depreciation and power costs, but labour hours do not measure machine use. Machine-intensive jobs would carry too little overhead and be under-priced, so a machine hour rate would be better.

explanation: One mark for each point.
hints: What causes the overhead after the new machines are bought?

stem:
Mutare Cabinets has a Cutting department (machine intensive) and a Finishing department (labour intensive). Budgeted figures for 2026:

| Department | Overhead US\$ | Budgeted activity |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Cutting | 40,500 | 4,500 machine hours |
| Finishing | 22,500 | 7,500 direct labour hours |

Job K12 (a wardrobe) uses direct materials of US\$680, 22 direct labour hours in Finishing at US\$5.50 an hour and 7 machine hours in Cutting. A mark-up of 25% on total production cost is added to find the selling price.

parts.label: (a)

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the absorption rate for Finishing, per direct labour hour.

parts.label: (c)

parts.label: (d)

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the selling price of Job K12.

parts.label: (f)

points.description: Cutting is machine intensive, so machine use causes its overhead
Finishing is labour intensive, so labour hours cause its overhead

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In Cutting the machines cause the overhead, so machine hours are used; in Finishing the workers cause it, so direct labour hours are used.

explanation: This item tests departmental absorption rates, a job cost and a cost-plus price.
hints: Rate = budgeted overhead ÷ budgeted activity of the department.

Chinhoyi Metalworks budgets production overheads of US\$70,000 for 2026, 14,000 direct labour hours and 8,750 machine hours. Two jobs for school desks were costed in January:

|  | Job P | Job Q |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Direct labour hours | 30 | 8 |
| Machine hours | 5 | 20 |

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the overhead absorbed by Job P using:

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the overhead absorbed by Job Q using:

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The owner says: The base does not matter, because the same total overhead is absorbed. Evaluate this statement using the two jobs.

points.description: Under labour hours Job P carries US\$150 and Job Q US\$40
Under machine hours the position reverses: P US\$40 and Q US\$160
So the base changes the cost of each job and the price quoted, although the total is the same
The base should match the cause of the overhead; here the machines probably cause it, so machine hours are fairer if the factory is mechanised

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The total is the same, but the share is not. Labour hours put US\$150 on P and US\$40 on Q; machine hours put US\$40 on P and US\$160 on Q. The base therefore changes costs and prices and should follow what causes the overhead.

hints: Compare the cost of each job under each base.

explanation: This item compares two absorption bases for labour-intensive and machine-intensive jobs.
